subject: Latent variable parameterization for probit regression

messages.author: 89df6cb36c324fe3
messages.subject: Latent variable parameterization for probit regression
parts:
Hi folks,

I am interested in fitting a joint model involving a binary outcome and another (say, continuous) outcome which depends on the latent variable of the binary outcome itself. As a concrete albeit contrived example, may the data generation mechanism is as follows:

rm(list = ls())
library(TMB)
library(mvtnorm)

set.seed(1219)

n <- 500
X1 <- cbind(1, rnorm(n))
true_beta <- c(0.5,1)
true_kappa <- c(-0.5,1)
true_eta <- X1 %*% true_beta

latent_err <- rnorm(n, mean = true_eta, sd = 1)
y1 <- as.numeric(latent_err > 0)
y2 <- rnorm(n, mean = cbind(1,latent_err - true_eta) %*% true_kappa, sd = 1)

and I observe X1, y1, and y2. 

Can the above model be fitted in TMB? In particular, I am not sure how to code in the equivalent version of "as.numeric(latent_err > 0)". At the same time, I recognize that the latent variable itself is truncated due to the binary nature of y1, and I am unsure if poses further issues with using the Laplace approximation (and whether there is a way to get around it!). 

Obviously if I ignore y2, then I could directly code in a probit regression e.g.,
     "
     #include <math.h> 
     #include <TMB.hpp> 
     #include <boost/accumulators/statistics/density.hpp>
     template<class Type>
 
     Type objective_function<Type>::operator() () 
          { 
          using namespace density;
          using namespace Eigen;
          
          DATA_VECTOR(y1); 
          DATA_MATRIX(X1); 
          int n = y1.size(); 
          
          
          PARAMETER_VECTOR(beta); 
          //PARAMETER_VECTOR(latent_err); 

          vector<Type> eta1 = X1 * beta;
          vector<Type> mu1 = pnorm(eta1, Type(0), Type(1));
          
          Type nll = -sum(dbinom(y1, Type(1), mu1, true)); 
          return nll;  
          }
          "

but the joint model or the latent variable parameterization is what I am looking for.

Much appreciated.

Yours non-significantly,
FH

messages.author: 02e03030784aa6a7
messages.subject: Re: Latent variable parameterization for probit regression
parts:
Hi, 

I think you are right that the Laplace approximation
will not work in this model, because the posterior
density of latent_err is not well approximated by a Gaussian. 
The easiest fix is to change the data generating mechanism 
(if acceptable) to something like:

invlogit <- exp(latent_err)/(1+exp(latent_err))
y1 <- rbinom(1,1,invlogit)

This should at least work in context of a joint model.
There may be other solutions that I do not see right now.

Hans

messages.author: 89df6cb36c324fe3
messages.subject: Re: Latent variable parameterization for probit regression
parts:
Thanks for your swift response Hans,

As you hinted at, unfortunately I do not think the suggestion will be suitable for the data generation mechanism I am thinking about, since it effectively turns the problem from y1 coming from a binary regression into a binary GLMM with a random intercept that has a known variance component of 1.

No worries, I will consider using EM-ing or MCMC-ing my way out of the problem instead.

Cheerio.

Yours non-significantly,
FH

messages.author: 02e03030784aa6a7
messages.subject: Re: [TMB users] Re: Latent variable parameterization for probit regression
parts:
You do not need to fix the variance at 1. If you use
invlogit <- exp(b*latent_err)/(1+exp(b*latent_err))
y1 <- rbinom(1,1,invlogit)

you can either choose b large (in the limit b=\infty you get the model you seek) or even try to estimate b (may be difficult).

Hans

messages.author: 89df6cb36c324fe3
messages.subject: Re: [TMB users] Re: Latent variable parameterization for probit regression
parts:
Thanks Hans,

If the variance component is unknown then the model is unidentifiable [known problem is binary GLMMs with observation specific random effects, because the binary relationship].

Your suggested approach is a good idea, although if the data generation mechanism was something like

b <- 1e6
latent_err <- rnorm(n, mean = true_eta, sd = 1)

y1 <- rbinom(n, 1, probit(1e6*latent_err))

Then the question again arises of how well the Laplace approximation on latent_err would work in this case if b is that large, since there is "effectively" a truncation.

Cheerio.

Yours non-significantly,
FH
